analysis.one_liner: Caps federal spending and cuts it one percent each year until it balances the budget, with automatic across-the-board cuts to enforce it.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Budget Committee on March 13, 2013, and never advanced; no vote was ever held and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a hard ceiling on most federal spending, starting at about $3.3 trillion in 2014 and shrinking by 1% each year, then fixed at 19% of the economy from 2017 onward. If Congress's actual spending exceeded the ceiling, automatic across-the-board cuts — explicitly including Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, which are normally exempt from such cuts — would take effect to bring spending back under the limit. It would also bar either chamber from considering any bill that would push spending past the cap, waivable only by a two-thirds vote. The bill never left the Senate Budget Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the bill would primarily benefit people who want a smaller federal government and lower future tax burdens, since the entire adjustment would come from spending cuts with no tax increases. Advocates would argue future taxpayers and anyone worried about debt and interest costs also gain. The bill itself would concentrate enormous budgetary power in automatic sequestration formulas and the Office of Management and Budget, which would decide each year's cuts, while Congress's own ability to spend would be sharply constrained.

how_it_helps.text: It would cap federal spending at about $3.3 trillion (less net interest) for 2014 and cut the cap 1% each year through 2016, aiming to balance the budget through spending cuts rather than tax increases.

After 2016, total outlays would be capped at 19% of GDP — roughly the 40-year historical average for revenue — which the bill's sponsors argue would end the annual deficit once revenues reach that level.

It would enforce the caps with automatic across-the-board sequestration and make it out of order in either chamber to consider legislation that breaches the current cap, waived only by a two-thirds vote.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on beneficiaries of federal programs, because the automatic cuts would reach Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid — a uniform percentage cut that spreads reductions across health care, retirement, defense, and every other area of spending without any legislative judgment about what is worth cutting.

drawbacks.text: The bill expressly waives the normal sequestration exemptions for Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, so automatic across-the-board cuts would fall on those programs rather than being confined to defense and discretionary accounts.

Spending is capped at 19% of GDP for 2017 and every year after, regardless of recessions, demographic aging, or emergencies, and the cut of 1% per year compounds, with no design for economic downturns.
Points of order and a two-thirds vote requirement in both chambers would make it very hard for a future Congress to respond to changed circumstances by raising spending, locking in the caps.
Enforcement relies on automatic sequestration by OMB and the President rather than on Congress voting on the specific cuts, shifting real budget decisions to an automatic formula.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal of putting federal debt on a sustainable path is legitimate, but the mechanism is poorly designed: a rigid formula that cuts spending 1% every year regardless of recessions, wars, or demographics, enforced by automatic across-the-board sequestration that includes Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid. Honest supporters would acknowledge the bill balances the budget not by reforming entitlements (its stated purpose) but by threatening indiscriminate cuts, and honest opponents would acknowledge the debt problem it cites is real. There are better-targeted ways to slow spending growth than a mechanical cap that cannot distinguish a bad program from a popular retirement benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Budget Committee from the day it was introduced; the committee never acted on it, no vote was ever scheduled, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Enzi on March 13, 2013, with five Republican cosponsors: Paul, Rubio, Vitter, Barrasso, and Isakson.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Budget, the standard first stop for spending-cap legislation.
No further action appears in the record — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Programs that would have absorbed the automatic cuts — Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, and defense — kept their funding, and anyone who opposed across-the-board spending cuts benefited from the bill never reaching a vote.

for.name: Sen. Michael Enzi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 13, 2013 and referred it to the Senate Budget Committee, where it received no further action.

for.name: Sens. Rand Paul, Marco Rubio, David Vitter, John Barrasso, and Johnny Isakson
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators signed on and no Democrat supported it.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats or independents supported the bill, and it never advanced in the Democratic-controlled Senate.

industries.industry: Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid beneficiaries and providers
industries.note: The bill removes the standard exemptions that protect these programs from sequestration, so the automatic 1%-per-year cuts would fall directly on retirement, health, and low-income benefit payments. Hospitals, doctors, and nursing homes that bill these programs would also absorb the payment reductions.

Defense is not exempt from the caps, so Pentagon spending would fall along with everything else; but many other government services would also shrink, and debt-service pressure eases. The bill does not single defense out for protection.

Balancing the budget entirely through spending cuts rather than taxes spares high earners from any revenue side of the ledger; the bill's findings pointly note revenues were 'scheduled to rise' above the historical average, implying no tax increases are needed.
